Model Response:

Opinion | In Defense of Wage Stagnation: The Unsung Hero Keeping Your “Dreams” Manageable

There’s a growing movement of people who, for reasons best understood by therapists and lottery-ticket vendors, refuse to accept the calming stability of stagnant wages. These “wage growth enthusiasts” keep insisting that pay should rise with productivity, inflation, or—this is my favorite—“the cost of living.”

The cost of living? As if living were some kind of subscription service your employer is obligated to renew.

Let me be clear: I fully support wage stagnation. Not because it’s perfect, but because it’s reliable. In a chaotic world of shifting weather patterns, volatile markets, and unpredictable human joy, stagnant wages are the one thing you can count on to stay exactly where they are—like a beloved family heirloom, or a ceiling fan in a rental apartment.

The Problem With Wage-Hike People: They Keep Wanting Things

Critics of wage stagnation often say things like:

  • “People deserve to share in the value they create.”
  • “Wages should keep up with inflation.”
  • “Why is everything getting more expensive but my paycheck isn’t?”

And to that I say: have you considered simply wanting less?

This is what wage intervention advocates don’t understand: stagnant wages aren’t a failure of the system. They’re an important feature that helps maintain the delicate balance between human ambition and corporate comfort. If wages rose, workers might start expecting other “radical” changes—like predictable schedules, paid leave, or chairs.

Chairs! In the workplace! Next they’ll ask for walls.

“But I Can’t Afford Rent”—A Stunning Personal Choice

One common complaint is that rent has increased while wages haven’t. This is a classic misunderstanding of economics.

Rent goes up because landlords are entrepreneurs, bravely innovating the concept of charging more. Wages stay flat because employers are also entrepreneurs, bravely innovating the concept of not paying more.

This is equilibrium. This is harmony. This is capitalism performing a beautiful duet titled “Not My Problem.”

If someone can’t afford rent, they should consider sensible alternatives, such as:

  • Moving somewhere cheaper (like 2004)
  • Getting roommates (like 2004)
  • Living with family (like 2004)
  • Becoming a “digital nomad” (like 2004, but with a laptop and lower serotonin)

Intervention? You Mean… Effort?

The most unrealistic demand from wage stagnation critics is “intervention.” They want policies. Reforms. Labor protections. Sometimes they even want unions—groups of workers coordinating together, as if they’re a sports team or, worse, a community.

But intervention sets a dangerous precedent: it implies society can solve problems.

Today it’s “raise wages.” Tomorrow it’s “make healthcare affordable” or “ensure childcare exists” or “stop the planet from becoming a convection oven.” Where does it end? With a functioning social contract?

Hard pass.

The Emotional Benefits of Stagnant Wages

Wage stagnation offers countless psychological advantages:

1) Builds character.
Nothing builds grit like choosing between dental care and vegetables.

2) Encourages creativity.
People become remarkably innovative when asked to make dinner out of rice and optimism.

3) Prevents arrogance.
If workers made enough to feel secure, they might develop “self-worth,” which is historically correlated with asking for things.

4) Keeps expectations realistic.
A stagnant wage is a gentle reminder that you are not the main character. You are supporting cast in the economy’s long-running drama, Shareholder Value: The Musical.

“But Productivity Has Increased!”

Yes, and look at you, noticing trends. Adorable.

Critics love pointing out that productivity has risen while wages have not. This is usually presented like it’s some kind of gotcha—as if the economy should reward increased output with increased compensation.

That’s a very sweet idea, like leaving cookies out for Santa or thinking “loyalty” means anything outside a dog.

Productivity gains are important because they prove we can do more with less—specifically, more work with less pay. That’s the dream. That’s efficiency. That’s the kind of innovation you can really put on a quarterly earnings call.

“People Need a Living Wage”

This phrase—living wage—is where the anti-stagnation crowd really shows its hand. It implies wages should be connected to life.

That’s an extreme position.

Wages are not for living. Wages are for participating. Living is a separate hobby, and frankly, one that’s gotten too expensive and should be downsized.

A “living wage” suggests society has some obligation to ensure that a full-time job can support basic needs. But if we start doing that, people might stop viewing survival as a personal branding exercise.

In Conclusion: Accept the Flatline

The truth is, wage stagnation is doing a lot of important work:

  • It keeps the economy exciting by turning every month into a puzzle.
  • It prevents workers from experiencing the moral hazard of comfort.
  • It encourages gratitude when someone finds a coupon.
  • It reminds everyone that the real raise was the friends you made along the way (at your second job).

So next time someone complains about stagnant wages, don’t engage with “data” or “empathy.” Just pat them gently on the shoulder and say:

“Have you tried adjusting your expectations to match the market?”

Then walk away confidently, secure in the knowledge that your paycheck will be there tomorrow—unchanged, unwavering, and blissfully indifferent.

Friends, neighbors, citizens—

We’ve been told, over and over, that when wages don’t rise on a neat, comforting schedule, it must mean something has “gone wrong.” That it’s evidence of failure. That it demands an emergency response—new rules, new agencies, new spending, new controls.

In a capitalist economy, it can be a normal feature—an expected phase—of a system that constantly adapts, competes, and reallocates resources. And if we want prosperity that lasts, we must resist the reflex to “fix” every uncomfortable reality with intervention.

Because here’s what capitalism actually is: not a promise that every number moves upward every year, but a process. A process that rewards productivity, innovation, skill, entrepreneurship, and risk. A process that disciplines inefficiency. A process that tells the truth—sometimes a hard truth—about what the economy can sustainably pay for, given competition at home and abroad.

When wages flatten, it can signal a dozen things: technology changing the value of certain tasks, global competition pressuring prices, consumers demanding cheaper goods, businesses facing tighter margins, or an economy shifting from one era to the next. Those forces aren’t moral failures. They are market signals. And market signals—however inconvenient—are information. Information we need.

So what happens when politicians decide they don’t like the information?

They try to override it.

They mandate outcomes instead of enabling opportunity. They try to force wages up by decree, or they drown employers in compliance costs, or they subsidize industries that should be evolving, or they inflate the currency and pretend it’s prosperity. And the result is so predictable it’s practically a law of political physics: fewer jobs, fewer hours, fewer openings for the inexperienced, fewer chances for small businesses to compete—while the biggest corporations hire the best lawyers and swallow the smaller players whole.

Intervention doesn’t eliminate trade-offs. It just hides them—until they come back more painful.

Let’s be honest about what many “solutions” to wage stagnation really are: they’re attempts to substitute political power for economic value creation. They’re efforts to treat the symptom by controlling the thermometer. They turn a dynamic economy into a regulated museum—safe from change, safe from competition, safe from the very pressure that produces progress.

And meanwhile, what do people actually need?

They need more ways to grow their value in the market. More pathways to skills. More competition among employers. More business formation. More investment. More innovation. More freedom to switch jobs, start companies, negotiate, train, learn, and build.

That’s not achieved by micromanaging wages from a capital city. It’s achieved by removing barriers that keep people from moving up.

If you want a society where wages rise sustainably, you don’t strangle the mechanism that raises them. You protect it.

You protect entrepreneurship—the ability of a person with an idea to challenge a giant.

The interconnectedness of economies through globalization places immense pressure on wages. Companies operate cross-border supply chains and face competitors from countries with vast differences in wage levels and labor regulations. Wage stagnation, therefore, acts as a stabilizing mechanism that enables industrial competitiveness on a global scale. It allows economies to adjust gradually to shifting comparative advantages and technological changes without abrupt shocks to employment. In essence, it balances the needs of labor, capital, and the broader economy, ensuring a sustainable basis for growth.

Capitalism thrives on innovation and efficiency, and wage discipline plays a crucial role in promoting these outcomes. Policies designed to artificially raise wages disrupt this feedback loop. Perhaps counterintuitively, wage stagnation contributes to preserving employment levels. Wage Stagnation: A Natural and Necessary Component of Global Capitalism

In recent decades, wage stagnation has sparked intense debate, with many policymakers advocating for government interventions and minimum wage hikes to boost worker incomes. However, examining the dynamics of global capitalism reveals that widespread wage stagnation is not only a natural consequence of economic forces but also an acceptable and necessary outcome to maintain competitiveness, spur innovation, and enhance overall efficiency. Opposing policies that artificially raise wages supports the long-term health of the economy and ultimately benefits society through sustained growth and opportunity.

Efficiency and Market-Driven Wage Setting

Fundamentally, wages are prices for labor, determined by market forces of supply and demand. When governments intervene to artificially inflate wages, they distort these signals, leading to inefficiencies such as decreased employment opportunities and misallocation of resources. If an abundant labor supply drives wages to plateau, this is a reflection of underlying economic realities, such as technological advances, automation, and global labor competition—forces that increase productivity and reduce the need for costly human labor. Accepting some degree of wage stagnation ensures that prices reflect true labor value, facilitating optimal allocation of capital and resources across sectors for maximum efficiency.

Global Competitiveness Requires Wage Flexibility

In a highly interconnected world economy, competitive advantage often hinges on cost structures. Emerging economies with abundant inexpensive labor have integrated into global supply chains, exerting downward pressure on wages worldwide. To maintain domestic industries’ competitiveness, containing labor costs becomes essential. Artificially raising wages can lead to job losses as firms either automate processes or offshore production to lower-wage countries, ultimately harming the very workers such policies aim to protect. Wage flexibility, including stagnant wages when appropriate, enables firms to adjust to international competition while maintaining employment levels and market share.

Incentivizing Innovation and Capital Allocation

Wage stagnation can incentivize productivity-enhancing innovation. When firms face pressure to contain labor costs, they are more likely to invest in new technologies and processes that drive productivity gains, boosting economic growth. If policies artificially raise wages independently of productivity, businesses may face reduced incentives or financial capacity to innovate. By allowing market-driven wage trends, economies ensure that capital is allocated towards activities that maximize growth potential rather than merely meeting politically determined wage floors.

Fostering a Stable and Sustainable Economic Environment

Trying to outpace productivity growth with forced wage increases risks stoking inflation and undermining macroeconomic stability. Historical evidence shows that when wages rise faster than productivity, economies can face competitiveness erosion, current account deficits, and eventually, reduced growth or crises. Conversely, wage moderation aligned with productivity advances fosters stable, long-run economic expansion built on solid fundamentals.

Conclusion

While concerns about inequality and worker welfare are legitimate, widespread wage stagnation is a natural product of globalization and technological progress within capitalism. It reflects real economic forces that bolster competitiveness and efficiency. Attempts to artificially override these forces through well-intentioned policies often backfire by increasing unemployment, fueling inflation, or reducing investment. Instead, policymakers should focus on complementary measures—such as education, training, and innovation promotion—that enhance productivity and create new opportunities, allowing wages to rise sustainably. Embracing wage stagnation not as a curse but as a necessary adjustment ensures continued economic vitality in a rapidly evolving global marketplace.

Certainly. The notion that wage stagnation for most workers is an unavoidable — or even a necessary — aspect of free market economies is often justified through several economic arguments. These explanations highlight how suppressed wage growth can, in theory, contribute to corporate growth, technological innovation, and economic stability. Here are the main reasons and supposed benefits:

1. Enhancing Corporate Competitiveness and Profitability

  • Cost Control: When wages remain flat, firms can contain labor costs, which typically represent a significant expense. Lower labor costs boost profit margins, offering resources for strategic investments.
  • Global Competition: Suppressed wage growth helps domestic companies remain competitive internationally by keeping production costs down compared to countries with cheaper labor.

2. Facilitating Investment and Innovation

  • Greater Capital for Technology: Higher profits (due to lower wage expense) can be reinvested into research and development, driving technological innovation that benefits overall productivity and economic growth.
  • Shift towards Technological Efficiency: If wages rise slowly relative to productivity, firms are incentivized to deploy capital toward automation and other technological solutions, which can ultimately raise output and efficiency.

3. Enabling Job Creation and Market Flexibility

  • Labor Market Flexibility: Wage stagnation can help maintain relatively low unemployment levels, as firms are more willing to hire when wages do not rise dramatically, keeping labor markets dynamic.
  • Absorbing Economic Shocks: In downturns, stagnant or flexible wages can enable firms to avoid layoffs, moderating unemployment fluctuations and aiding faster recovery.

4. Moderating Inflationary Pressures

  • Controlled Consumer Prices: Slower wage growth restrains consumer demand from overheating, helping prevent demand-pull inflation.
  • Price Stability: Since wage growth feeds into overall production costs, flat wages help stabilize prices, supporting purchasing power stability for consumers broadly.

5. Supporting Capital Formation and Broader Economic Growth

  • Increased Savings and Investment: Higher corporate profits (sometimes instead of higher wages) ostensibly lead to greater savings and investment, fueling infrastructure, technology, and capacity expansion.
  • Resource Allocation Efficiency: Wage flexibility allows markets to allocate economic resources more efficiently, rewarding high-skill, high-productivity sectors while limiting resources to less productive activities.

Summary

In essence, accepting wage stagnation as part of a free market framework is sometimes rationalized by suggesting it

  • keeps companies profitable and competitive,
  • channels resources toward technological upgrades,
  • helps stabilize employment,
  • limits inflation,
  • and encourages investment and economic expansion.

Important Note

While these are the theoretical justifications, it is important to recognize they are subject to significant debate. Critics argue that persistent wage stagnation undermines aggregate demand, worsens inequality, and dampens long-term growth prospects. Nonetheless, the above points represent the common reasoning behind viewing limited wage growth as an intrinsic — and arguably functional — feature of many free market economies.
